Cytokine modulating therapy includes blocking the action of tu- mour necrosis factor with adalimumab, etanercept, or infliximab, which have been found to be effective for psoriasis skin lesions and psoriatic arthritis. The British Association of Dermatologists recommends15 that in chronic plaque psoriasis the bio- logical therapies (efalizumab, etanercept, and inflixi- mab) should be reserved for patients with severe disease that is unresponsive or refractory to standard therapies such as acitretin, ciclosporin, methotrexate, UVB, and PUVA, or when such therapies cannot be used. Etaner- cept is considered to be the first choice in stable disease, infliximab may be useful when rapid disease control is needed such as in unstable erythrodermic or pustular psoriasis, and efalizumab should be used in patients with a high risk of latent tuberculosis or evidence of de- myelinating disease, as the other 2 drugs are contra- indicated in these patients. • Systemic retinoids such as acitretin are also effective, and use with PUVA may allow a reduction in doses and associated toxicity for each therapy. Generalised pustu- lar and palmoplantar pustular psoriasis are particularly responsive to acitretin. UVB therapy may also be used with acitretin. • Hydroxycarbamide, fumarates, tioguanine, and sul- fasalazine have also been tried. Many anecdotal reports note improvement of psoriasis when patients are given drug therapy for co-existing disease. The value of such drugs can be particularly difficult to establish because of the chronic relapsing and recurring nature of psoriasis. The chronic nature of psoriasis has resulted in a number of different strategies being tried in order to maximise treat- ment efficacy and minimise toxicity.5,6 Combinations of established drugs at lower doses can include methotrexate with either ciclosporin or acitretin, or acitretin with UV therapy. Sequential therapy uses a rapidly acting, poten- tially more toxic, drug to bring the condition under control initially, followed by a less toxic drug for maintenance; ex- amples include using methotrexate or ciclosporin followed by acitretin. Rotational therapy may be used to minimise long-term toxicity by using each treatment for 1 to 2 years; methotrexate, acitretin, and UV therapy have been used in this way.6 However, ciclosporin should not follow PUVA therapy in this way because of an increased risk of cutane- ous squamous cell carcinoma.5 There is limited experience with the use of newer immunomodulating drugs in these regimens.6 1.
